headline: A Democratic midterm sweep set off a violent AI-stock selloff, and a strong jobs report keeps a December Fed rate hike in view. Anthropic's IPO plans and a busy biopharma deal tape sit against that backdrop.

paragraphs.text: The political shift is the organizing theme. Democrats won Congress on Tuesday, and Endpoints, STAT and the New York Times are all working through what that means for the sector. STAT expects relief for hospitals, since Democrats are likely to try to reverse Medicaid cuts and widen coverage. Other pieces look at drug pricing, science funding, health equity programs and a likely tougher stance on healthcare fraud. In the meantime, states have filed another suit to delay Medicaid work requirements, days after a federal judge found that implementing them would cause irreparable harm. Separately, Calley Means, who just resigned from the administration, accused White House officials, Susie Wiles among them, of bending to industry and donors. These are early reads and allegations, not policy changes.

paragraphs.text: CMS kept issuing rules regardless. It codified the Medicare drug price negotiation framework from the Inflation Reduction Act, despite repeated industry court challenges. It proposed rolling back hospital Conditions of Participation, including Biden-era emergency department obstetric requirements, with estimated savings of $320 million. And it adopted a rule that ties Medicare billing privileges to owner conduct, including at parent companies. It also denied recertification to two No Surprises Act arbiters, which insurers welcomed, though both can appeal. A federal judge lifted CMS's freeze on new ACA broker registrations. For insurers, Humana beat on Q3 earnings and revenue and expects more Medicare Advantage membership growth in 2027, which addresses the enrollment worry that had weighed on the stock.

paragraphs.text: Deal flow was active. The Wall Street Journal reports AstraZeneca has offered about $10 billion for Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, and Fierce says at least three analyst teams think Rhythm will hold out and a bidding war is possible. ANI Pharmaceuticals proposed a $560 million purchase of Sweden's Egetis and its orphan drug Emcitate. Boehringer Ingelheim signed a potential $7.4 billion oncology deal with China's SBP Group, and Fresenius formed a 37-asset biosimilar collaboration with WuXi Biologics. On obesity, Lilly struck a deal for Hims & Hers to offer its branded weight-loss drugs, a change of course for Hims, which had sold knockoff GLP-1s. Lilly also made a compounding rival drop weight-loss claims. Fierce's new oral GLP-1 tracker shows Lilly's Foundayo setting a prescription record while Novo's Wegovy pill returned to its prior high. On financing, Rezera, formerly NodThera, is targeting a $181 million IPO to fund phase 3 work on an NLRP3 inhibitor, and LionBio raised a $6 million pre-seed for a nasal-spray GLP-1.

paragraphs.text: Safety and clinical news was mixed. Novartis disclosed more tumor cases in children given Zolgensma. STAT cites seven previously unreported cases, and BioPharma Dive counts nine in total, two with evidence that the viral vector integrated into patient DNA. That could raise questions across AAV gene therapy. Sarepta stopped enrolling its confirmatory phase 3 trial of Elevidys. Moderna's norovirus vaccine plans are in limbo after a phase 3 miss. On the positive side, Moderna posted a small profit and raised its outlook on Covid vaccine sales, with $1.3 billion in Q3 revenue far above estimates. J&J's Rybrevant won accelerated FDA approval in recurrent head and neck cancer. Amgen's Repatha was linked to fewer heart attacks. Immunocore reported early two-year survival data for a bispecific combination in uveal melanoma. Merck dropped a Sutro-partnered IL-2 drug.

paragraphs.text: The week was dominated by an AI-linked selloff. The Dow fell more than 1,800 points on Thursday and the Nasdaq Composite entered correction territory. The FT and WSJ tie the rout to Democrats' election victories, which fed anxieties already building, and the WSJ says systematic trades amplified the losses. Estimates of lost value run from $2.5 trillion (DealBook) to $3.2 trillion (FT). Friday brought a rebound: the Nasdaq 100 rose 1.4%, though the WSJ describes US stocks as mixed by the close and the FT calls the recovery feeble compared with past rebounds. The FT also says investors are no longer pricing in accelerating AI growth. MarketWatch's analysts warn of more volatility. SpaceX shares fell on fears of Democratic retribution against Musk, though Deutsche Bank says buy the dip.

paragraphs.text: Macro data pointed the other way. The US added 165,000 jobs in October, well ahead of forecasts, and unemployment fell to 4.1%. Professional and business services supplied 70,000 of the gains. The Fed held rates last week but a December hike is widely expected. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said Americans are on a treadmill of high inflation and more hikes are likely. The WSJ notes that a sustained AI selloff could argue against a move. October CPI is the key data point this coming week. Michigan sentiment improved to 51 from 48 but remains gloomy. The WSJ Dollar Index rose 0.46% on the week to 97.52.

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere, Eurozone retail sales fell as high energy prices hit confidence. Canada's unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, a six-month high. Thailand's inflation overshot its central bank's target on fuel costs tied to the Middle East conflict. Strong wage growth supports a Bank of Japan move in December. European governments face a two-way choice between Pablo Hernandez de Cos and Klaas Knot to succeed Lagarde at the ECB. In commodities, gold fell almost 7% in October to end the month below $4,000 an ounce, while China's central bank kept buying for a second year. Trafigura is buying copper in Asia as Chinese supply tightens and regional spot premiums reach records. China's foreign exchange reserves edged up in October.

paragraphs.text: On trade, the FT reports the US told China it must immediately meet the Busan deal terms, citing shortfalls on rare earths and critical products. China said it opposes US sanctions on two Chinese companies and reserves the right to respond. The New York Times reports Commerce approved dozens of Chinese firms to handle Nvidia H200 chips, some with questionable ties. The FT separately reports US intelligence concerns about a relationship between Nvidia's Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy. That is an allegation, so treat it cautiously.

paragraphs.text: The AI selloff is spilling into debt. CNBC says CoreWeave's bond yield has topped 16%, which it reads as stress in AI debt markets as investors worry about a data center slowdown. MarketWatch argues that data center borrowing overwhelmed investor portfolios this year and disappointed on performance. It adds that funding needs will not ease with Democrats controlling Congress, which is an opinion piece. Forbes warns that tight credit spreads may be hiding the next refinancing problem. With a Fed hike expected, the combination of heavy supply, stressed AI issuers and tight spreads is the risk to watch. The FT's Alphaville also ran a piece on the flight to quality, but only the headline is visible.

paragraphs.text: Private credit looks steadier for now. Bloomberg says private credit's software loans are holding up against early AI disruption, though the word early matters. Partners Group is a recurring subject: ad-hoc-news says it raised a $510 million credit feeder and is expanding in Abu Dhabi and European infrastructure, but still faces stubborn US redemption pressure ahead of a fund vote. These are secondary summaries, so details are limited. In India, TVS Capital entered private credit with a 750 crore rupee fund. Goldman Sachs Asset Management published an alternatives survey on LP views, but the list gives no findings. Ark Invest is pitching tokenized, exchange-traded interval funds with venture exposure, which Alphaville treats skeptically. A new ETF mixes high-yield debt, emerging market debt and CLOs.

paragraphs.text: Distress items were scattered. Holyrood is exploring seizing assets of Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance to prioritize Scottish government claims over other creditors, which is a reminder that governments can compete with lenders in a restructuring. In Paraguay, President Santiago Peña was impeached, removed and placed under house arrest after a bank with close administration ties collapsed. The New York Times describes the Odyssey endless cruise as undone by secrecy, debt and fuel costs. California ordered crypto ATM firm CoinFlip to pay $4.8 million to scam victims.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO is the main equity capital markets story, and the reports conflict. The FT says it is pressing ahead to list before Thanksgiving, targeting a $1.5 trillion valuation, and lining up a UK retail offer. The WSJ says it may scale back the offering. FXLeaders says buyers are eyeing about $1.1 trillion. Bloomberg calls the IPO AI's true reckoning, and Kalshi odds on it have fallen. The FT also notes the SpaceX slide may dent demand. The valuation range and size are the numbers to watch. Separately, the New York Times reports suspicious, well-timed bets on Polymarket and Kalshi before a Times/Siena poll release, though it is unclear whether the trader had inside information.
